outcome: No source found since 26 January 2024 settles or moves the infinitude question: the only in-window item is a Lean 4 formalisation (arXiv:2601.07444, submitted 12 Jan 2026) that restates the definition and checks two known pairs, and no source states whether infinitely many betrothed pairs exist or are known.
problem_asks: Whether there are infinitely many betrothed numbers. Parts: (1) whether the set of betrothed numbers is infinite. A betrothed pair is two positive integers m and n with s(m) = n+1 and s(n) = m+1, where s(k) is the sum of the proper divisors of k; equivalently sigma(m) = sigma(n) = m+n+1. Each betrothed number has exactly one partner (n is determined by m as s(m)-1), so infinitely many betrothed numbers is equivalent to infinitely many betrothed pairs. Scope note: the statement does not say whether m and n must be distinct. If m = n were allowed, the condition s(m) = m+1 (sigma(m) = 2m+1) is the quasiperfect-number condition, none of which is known; the Wikipedia wording ('two positive integers') and the Lean paper ('two distinct') differ on this. The statement asks for no bound, no count, and nothing about parity. Parity of members (all known pairs have opposite parity) and whether same-parity pairs exist are adjacent open questions the statement does not ask.

events.what_happened: Peter Hagis Jr. and Graham Lord, 'Quasi-Amicable Numbers', Mathematics of Computation 31(138), 1977, pp. 608-611: the computational study that gave these numbers their first systematic enumeration (called quasi-amicable there, after Garcia 1968). Secondary sources credit it with the first 46 pairs; OEIS A126160 gives 46 pairs with m <= 10^7. The AMS page and PDF could not be opened (HTTP 403), so the paper's own statements are not read here.
events.delivers: A finite enumeration of pairs with the first member up to about 10^7 (46 pairs per OEIS A126160). Establishes finitely many instances only; says nothing about whether the set is infinite.
events.remains: All of problem_asks: whether the set of betrothed pairs (and so betrothed numbers) is infinite; whether same-parity pairs exist.

events.object: The pairs themselves, e.g. (48, 75), (140, 195), (1050, 1925). A finite list of explicit pairs; no argument about infinitude.

events.what_happened: Mitchell Dickerman's 1997 quasi-sociable chain: a cycle of eight reduced sociable numbers (first member 1215571544) under the map k -> s(k) - 1. Credited by the Wikipedia article 'Betrothed numbers' (which says quasi-sociable numbers generalise betrothed numbers) and by Jan Munch-Pedersen's table posting on primepuzzles.net (attributed 'R8 Dickerman 1997'). This is a chain of length eight, not a pair. The original 1997 publication was not located.
events.delivers: One eight-term quasi-sociable cycle. It establishes no betrothed pair, so it does not bear on whether there are infinitely many. Recorded as a neighbouring result.
events.directly_checkable: The cycle can be checked by iterating k -> s(k) - 1 on the listed members, which requires factoring each member; the source lists the factorisations.
events.doubts: Attribution rests on secondary sources (Wikipedia and a primepuzzles table page, the latter seen only as a search snippet). The original is not located.
events.direction: Does not bear on the question directly. It is a different object: a longer cycle of the same map.
events.object: An eight-term cycle of the reduced aliquot map, first term 1215571544, with prime factorisations given in the source. It is a quasi-sociable chain, not a betrothed pair.

events.what_happened: Paul Pollack, 'Quasi-Amicable Numbers are Rare', Journal of Integer Sequences 14 (2011), Article 11.5.2 (received 26 Nov 2010, published 21 Apr 2011). Theorem 1: the set of integers n belonging to a quasi-amicable (betrothed) pair has asymptotic density zero, stated with an upper-density bound involving the iterate of the aliquot sum. The introduction says earlier work was mainly empirical and that the data 'suggests that the number of such pairs with a member <= N tends to infinity with N, albeit very slowly'. No arXiv or earlier preprint was found in searches.
events.revisions: No earlier preprint found; the journal version is taken as the first public written argument.
events.delivers: The set of members of betrothed pairs has asymptotic density zero. This restricts how thin the set is. It does not decide whether the set is infinite, since density-zero sets can be infinite. The introduction's numerical observation is empirical and is not a proof.
events.remains: Whether the set is infinite, i.e. whether infinitely many betrothed pairs exist. Same-parity existence and parity structure are not addressed.

checked_by.qualification: Peer-reviewed journal; author is a university number theorist (Paul Pollack, listed at the University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign on the journal page)

events.direction: Neutral on infinitude. A density result within the integers; the problem's quantity, the count of pairs, is not settled and not moved as a bound.

events.what_happened: Comment by Harvey P. Dale on the OEIS entry for the larger member of a betrothed pair (A003503), dated 7 Apr 2013: all known betrothed pairs have opposite parity; if a < b is a betrothed pair with a and b of the same parity, then a > 10^10. The entry attributes the 10^10 bound to Hagis & Lord (1977).
events.delivers: A computational lower bound (10^10) on the smaller member of any same-parity pair. It constrains where such pairs could sit; it does not show they exist or do not, and says nothing about infinitude.
events.remains: All of problem_asks; also whether same-parity pairs exist at all.
events.doubts: Unrefereed OEIS comment. The entry attributes the bound to Hagis & Lord (1977); I did not locate its derivation. Wikipedia gives 10^13 for the same statement (see disputes).
events.direction: Neutral on infinitude. A bound on the same-parity case, which the problem does not ask.

events.what_happened: Comment by David A. Corneth on OEIS A003503, dated 26 Jan 2019. (i) For a betrothed pair (k, m), sigma(k) = sigma(m); this follows immediately from the defining equations. (ii) If k and m are odd, both are squares; if both are even, each is a square or twice a square (not necessarily from the same family). (iii) 'Using inspection and the results above', the minimal term of a same-parity pair exceeds 2 x 10^14.
events.delivers: Structural restrictions on same-parity pairs (square conditions) and a computational lower bound of 2 x 10^14 on their minimal term, justified by inspection. It establishes no existence and no infinitude result. Its bound is a finite search statement.
events.remains: All of problem_asks; also whether same-parity pairs exist and whether the square conditions can be met at all.
events.directly_checkable: The sigma equality in (i) is a one-line check from the definitions. The square conditions in (ii) can be tested on any candidate pair.
events.doubts: The bound in (iii) is justified only by 'inspection' in the comment; no written derivation is given. Search summaries report that the comment itself says the cases are not fully resolved; I did not verify that sentence in the entry.
events.direction: Neutral on infinitude. Constrains the same-parity case, which the problem does not ask.

events.what_happened: Zhipeng Chen, Haolun Tang and Jingyi Zhan (Shanghai Dianji University), 'Formalization of Amicable Numbers Theory', arXiv:2601.07444, submitted 12 Jan 2026 (v1, the only version listed). A Lean 4 development on Mathlib, reported as 2076 lines and 139 theorems. Section 2.2 defines betrothed numbers and states that they are a relaxation of amicable pairs; the smallest pair (48,75) is noted. Section 3.7.1 formalises IsBetrothedPair (s m = n+1 and s n = m+1) and says the pairs (48,75) and (140,195) were verified computationally. The paper also lists sociable numbers and parity-constraint theorems among its extensions; the parity theorems it describes concern amicable pairs. Repository: https://github.com/chainstart/amicable-numbers (Apache 2.0).
events.delivers: A formal statement of the betrothed-pair definition and machine checks of two known pairs, (48,75) and (140,195). It establishes no new pair, no infinitude result and no parity result for betrothed numbers.

machine_checked.note: The paper claims 'zero sorry placeholders' in several places. Not verified: the Lean source was not read directly. The paper's Section 3.7.4 says 'We formalize (without proof) deep theorems about the parity structure of amicable pairs' and later 'These theorems are proven using 2-adic valuation arguments'. The verification of (220,284) uses native_decide (Sections 3.3 and 4.1), which adds the Lean.ofReduceBool axiom beyond the kernel; the paper does not discuss this.

events.directly_checkable: The two pairs can be checked by hand: sigma(48) = sigma(75) = 124 and sigma(140) = sigma(195) = 336, with 48+75+1 = 124 and 140+195+1 = 336.
events.doubts: (a) Internal inconsistency on sorry-free and proven status, as in machine_checked. (b) The repository README lists 'formal statements' of three open conjectures, including InfinitelyManyAmicableConj for amicable pairs; if stated as theorems these would need placeholders, which I did not confirm in source. (c) The paper's Code Availability section describes AmicableLib/ and Amicable/ directories; the repository tree as fetched shows only Amicable/ (Basic.lean, Examples.lean, Thabit.lean) and a root Amicable.lean, and no betrothed file was located. These observations come from WebFetch summaries of GitHub pages, not from the files. (d) No review by a named mathematician was found.
events.direction: Neutral on the question. A formal restatement of the definition and two known instances; does not bear on whether infinitely many pairs exist.

disputes.summary: Same-parity bound. Wikipedia (raw wikitext) says any pair of the same parity must exceed 10^13. OEIS A003503 (Dale 2013) says the smaller member must exceed 10^10, attributed to Hagis & Lord 1977. Corneth (2019) gives a minimal term above 2 x 10^14, by inspection. These are not reconciled; the Wikipedia figure may be a weaker statement or an older one. The problem does not ask this, so the discrepancy does not change the infinitude record.

Early pairs. The CRC entry, as reported in a search snippet and not opened, gives (1050, 1575) and (1648, 1925). Wikipedia, MathWorld and OEIS A005276 give (1050, 1925) and (1575, 1648). Checked by hand: sigma(1050) = 2976 gives partner 2976 - 1050 - 1 = 1925; sigma(1575) = 3224 gives partner 3224 - 1575 - 1 = 1648. The Wikipedia/OEIS pairing is arithmetically correct.

Author and count attributions. Beck and Wajar (1993) is spelled Najar in the scan's OCR, in MathWorld and in Pollack's bibliography. The 46 pairs are attributed to Hagis & Lord (1977) and the next 33 to Beck & Wajar (1993) only in secondary sources; neither original was read in usable form. Dickerman's 1997 chain is attributed in Wikipedia and in a table posting; the original was not located.

summary: Sources opened: the Wikipedia article 'Betrothed numbers' and its raw wikitext; the OEIS entries A005276, A003503 and A126160; the Chen-Tang-Zhan arXiv preprint 2601.07444 (abstract, HTML) and its GitHub repository (README and directory tree); Pollack's 2011 paper (journal page and TeX source via the EMIS mirror); MathWorld's pages for the betrothed and quasiamicable entries; Futility Closet (29 Sep 2025); erdosproblems.com problem 830 (the amicable-pair analogue); and Dimitrov arXiv 2408.07387 (HTML). The Wikipedia article defines betrothed pairs (s(m) = n+1 and s(n) = m+1, equivalently sigma(m) = sigma(n) = m+n+1), lists six pairs, says all known pairs have opposite parity, and gives the same-parity bound above 10^13. It says nothing about whether infinitely many pairs exist, and it carries no open-problem or unsolved wording. OEIS A003503 and A126160 and MathWorld are also silent on infinitude. The Futility Closet post calls the parity question open, but cites nothing and is not a result. Guy's Unsolved Problems in Number Theory, section B5, is the likely origin of the question; it covers quasi-amicable or betrothed numbers, but I could not open it, so I cannot confirm its exact wording or whether it poses infinitude as open. Closest mathematics: Pollack (2011) proves that the set of members of such pairs has asymptotic density zero, and notes that the data suggest the count of pairs with a member at most N tends to infinity, 'albeit very slowly'. That is empirical, and density zero is compatible with infinitely many pairs, so it does not move the question. The computational events (Hagis & Lord 1977; Beck & Wajar 1993; Resta's count of 4122 pairs with m up to 10^13 in 2019) are finite instances and do not bear on infinitude. Corneth's 2019 OEIS comment gives square conditions on same-parity pairs and a bound of 2 x 10^14 by inspection; again finite or structural, with no existence claim. The one in-window event is the Lean formalisation arXiv:2601.07444 (12 Jan 2026). It defines the betrothed pair and checks two known pairs; it adds no pair and no infinitude or parity theorem for betrothed numbers. Its parity theorems concern amicable pairs. Its sorry-free status is inconsistent within the paper ('zero sorry placeholders' versus 'We formalize (without proof)' in Section 3.7.4), and I did not read the Lean files to settle it. The repository's formal open-conjecture list includes InfinitelyManyAmicableConj for amicable pairs, which shows the formalisers treat the amicable infinitude question as open, but that is a different question. The Erdos problem 830 page, the amicable analogue, lists infinitude of amicable pairs as open, last edited 28 Sep 2025, and does not mention betrothed numbers. Close calls: (1) I recorded the Lean paper as an event because it is the only in-window item that uses this problem's object, while its delivers is definitional only. (2) I treated Pollack's density result as not moving the problem, because the problem asks about infinitude, not density. (3) I treated the finite counts as non-moving under the scope test in section 2.1. (4) I took 'distinct' as implicit in the problem, because the Lean paper and the standard definition use distinct pairs; the Wikipedia wording says 'two positive integers'. Allowing m = n would bring in the quasiperfect condition, which is also unknown. AI: no source names any AI system in connection with betrothed numbers. Searches for AI results in number theory (GPT-5.x Pro work on Erdos problems and the unit-distance result, AlphaEvolve and FunSearch on aliquot or amicable numbers, the Erdos-problem trackers, Claude or Anthropic with amicable numbers) returned nothing that mentions betrothed or quasi-amicable pairs. The Lean paper and its README contain no AI mention. ai.none_found is therefore true on every event.
competing_reading: Someone could say the in-window Lean formalisation is progress because it moves the problem from informal to machine-checked for the two known pairs and the definition. That reading treats formalisation of the setting as a result on the question, and it does not change whether infinitely many pairs exist. A second reading: the density-zero theorem and the count data could be read as strong evidence for a finite answer, but the sources themselves say the count grows with N and the density is compatible with infinitude. A third reading counts the question as partly settled because same-parity pairs are constrained (Corneth 2019, Dale 2013); the statement does not ask about parity, so that reading would widen the problem beyond its statement.
what_would_settle_it: (1) The text of Guy, Unsolved Problems in Number Theory, section B5 (2nd ed. pp. 59-60, 3rd ed. pp. 91-92), to confirm that infinitude is the posed question and that it is marked open there. (2) A readable copy of Hagis & Lord 1977 (AMS PDF) and Beck & Wajar 1993 (Fibonacci Quarterly) to confirm counts and attributions. (3) Reading the Lean source files at github.com/chainstart/amicable-numbers for sorry, native_decide and IsBetrothedPair, which would settle sorry-free status. (4) A full-text arXiv search for 'betrothed' and 'quasi-amicable' after 12 Jan 2026; the search tool did not return any such post, but it cannot browse arXiv listings. (5) Any published result that proves or disproves infinitude, which none of the sources shows.
